title: Raised by the river
hook: a king's daughter is raised by fishermen, and the epic's own answer to what makes a person
carry: conduct, not birth, shows who you are

segments.voice: Yesterday: a father's boon, death only with his son's leave, and the water Hindus still offer him. He had no child, so Hindus offer him water.

A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell. He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river. This is where Satyavati's story begins.
screen: `A HAWK OVER THE YAMUNA.` → `A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.` → `IT FALLS INTO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls. Some time later, fishermen catch her, and inside they find two human children, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends, and she rises back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king, and the king makes a choice. He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be King Matsya. The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen: let her be your daughter. She grows up on the river, carrying the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati. Remember what she told Shantanu: I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen. Every word true. Now see where the poem takes her. This fisher girl becomes a queen of the Kurus, and the great-grandmother of the cousins the great war is about. Her first son will be Vyasa, the sage Hindus honor for arranging the Vedas and telling this very epic. Many teachers point to it: the greatest teacher in the story is a fisherwoman's son. And the epic says it outright, later on. A serpent asks Prince Yudhishthira who is truly a Brahmin. His answer: look for truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct. If those are in someone born low and missing in someone born high, birth doesn't decide it. India's history has also ranked people by birth, by caste, and that has done real harm; many Hindu saints and reformers have pushed back, pointing to stories like these.
screen: `TWINS FOUND IN A FISH.` · `LET HER BE YOUR DAUGHTER.` · `A FISHER GIRL BECOMES A QUEEN.` · `WHO IS TRULY A BRAHMIN?` · then, large: `CONDUCT, NOT BIRTH.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu rites, the priest asks your name and your gotra, your family line. Today, say your own line quietly: your name, then the people who raised you, by blood or by love, as far back as you know. Then add one quality you want people to find in you: truth, patience, kindness. In this epic, that counts too.
Satyavati. A king's daughter raised as a fisherman's own, and mother of the sage the Vedas come through.
Your line: conduct, not birth, shows who you are. Tomorrow, a boat on the river, and the son born on an island. Day seven hundred sixteen, done.

screen: `DAY 716 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VYASA, BORN ON AN ISLAND.`

howItsDone: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

notes: All paraphrase. Check in Ganguli's account of Uparichara: the seed caught on a leaf and sent by a hawk to his queen Girika; the second hawk; the fall into the Yamuna; Adrika, an apsara cursed by Brahma to be a fish; the twins found by fishermen; Adrika's release; the king keeping the boy (later King Matsya) and giving the girl to the fishermen's chief.

The king here is named Vasu (Uparichara); he is not one of the eight Vasus of days 704-709. The script calls him 'Vasu, called Uparichara' once and then Uparichara; a Keeper may prefer to use only Uparichara to avoid confusion.
Ganguli says she had the smell of fish from her association with fishermen; the script says only that she carries the smell of fish. The name Matsyagandha is left out.
'Some time later' replaces the text's term for when the fish was caught; no number is given.
Day 717 (already written) picks up with the ferry crossing, Parashara and the boon of fragrance; this day stops before the boat and does not explain the fragrance Shantanu followed on day 710.
